name: Beard vitamins (zinc, B-complex, D)

card.summary: Multivitamin-style stacks of zinc, B vitamins and vitamin D aimed at beard growth; deficiencies can affect hair, but no trials show extra vitamins thicken a beard.
card.note: Biotin can interfere with some lab tests; high vitamin D intake can be toxic.

quick.overview:
Some beard-growth routines include over-the-counter zinc, B-complex (often biotin) and vitamin D, on the idea that nutrient shortfalls limit facial hair.

Reference sources link deficiencies of some of these nutrients to hair thinning, but no clinical trials were found testing them for beard growth in people who are not deficient.
quick.mechanism: Zinc, biotin and other B vitamins are involved in skin and hair biology, and deficiency states are associated with hair changes. Whether supplementing beyond adequate intake changes beard growth has not been studied.
quick.risks: Biotin at 5 mg/day or more can distort thyroid and vitamin D lab results. Vitamin D toxicity, with high blood calcium, can occur at very high doses. Supplements in the US are not approved for effectiveness before sale.

lead: Beard-growth stacks sold or discussed online often combine zinc, B-complex vitamins (frequently biotin) and vitamin D. Deficiencies of some of these nutrients are associated with hair changes: zinc deficiency with thin, sparse hair, and biotin deficiency, which is rare, with hair thinning.[1][2]

Reference sources report that there are no randomized controlled trials proving biotin supplementation helps healthy people's hair, and general hair-loss references state that dietary supplements are not typically recommended.[1][4] No studies found address these vitamins specifically for beard growth.
infobox: Zinc, biotin and other B vitamins, vitamin D

paras: Zinc deficiency is described as causing alopecia ("thin and sparse hair"), skin problems and impaired taste or smell.[2] Biotin deficiency is rare in people eating a normal diet, and mild cases can cause hair thinning, brittle nails or a facial rash; most cases arise from a genetic condition, biotinidase deficiency.[1] Iron and vitamin B12 deficiencies are listed among less common causes of hair loss.[4]

Biotin supplements of 5 mg/day or more can interfere with immunoassays used for thyroid hormones and vitamin D levels, giving falsely normal or abnormal results; a 2017 FDA safety communication on this is cited.[1] Vitamin D toxicity is rare but occurs with high-dose supplements, causing high blood calcium; the US tolerable upper intake for adults is 4,000 IU/day.[3]
In the US supplements are not required to be approved for effectiveness before sale, and labels may carry structure/function claims with a disclaimer that the FDA has not evaluated them.[1]
No studies found for beard growth. Related general information: a review cited by Wikipedia found no randomized trials showing biotin supplementation helps hair in healthy people.[1]
